utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We continue with the cross-examination but this time by Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to ask you to begin with some questions about your testimony in chief. Now, in that testimony, when Dr. Karadzic asked you things like, tell us what was said about an incident, tell us what was said and what's being alleged about an incident, what was claimed about an incident, how an incident was portrayed, the answer you usually gave him was to summarise the evidence related to those sniping incidents, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way it was basically.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can barely hear the witness. Could he please be asked to speak closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you understand that, Mr. Poparic? The interpreters have trouble hearing you. So they are asking if you could lean a little bit closer to the microphone when you give your answers. And then when Dr. Karadzic would ask you, for example, to tell us what was officially said in the documents, you would do the same thing, you would summarise what the document said; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But actually, Mr. Poparic, you don't do that and you haven't done that completely, and you haven't always done that accurately, have you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I didn't understand your question. What does that mean, accurately? You mean did I interpret exactly the way things happened? I don't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When I ask you whether you did something accurately, I'm asking you whether or not you got it right or wrong. So when you summarise the evidence, you haven't always got it right, have you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that what I said was correct but I don't really understand what this refers to, whether I gave some additional comments. I mean, in addition to the summary. But basically I stand by what I said, that it was correct. Now, whether that qualifies as my comment or a summary, that is something I cannot precisely distinguish.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. I'll give you an example. You told the Court at transcript page 38964, that it was your opinion that sniping incident F6, which took place on the 6th of January, 1994, happened at around 4.30 that day and you said that that was on the basis of the testimony of the victim, Sanija Dzevlan. You told the Chamber at that same page that Mrs. Dzevlan claimed she had set out to visit her mother at the hospital at around 3.00 p.m. and the hospital was some ten minutes away. And your evidence on what might have been the visibility at 4.30 p.m. that date is based on your estimate of how long she would have spent visiting her mother in the hospital before she got shot. Do you remember that because it's paragraph 81 of your report at page 65 in English and 92 and 93 in your language. So you remember that analysis?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly. I do remember. I already said that the problem regarding that incident is that the exact time is unknown, when it happened. There are statements to the effect that it happened around 3.00 and then in another statement she said about 1630. So this incident occurred within that period of time, but what is important there is the time that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've answered part of my question, but if we can go further, I'd like to stay focused on my first question to you, which was about the accuracy of your summaries of the evidence. Now, you said that the witness claimed she had gone out to visit her mother in the hospital. In fact, her mother wasn't even in the hospital and she didn't go there to visit her, she went there to get medicine. And she said that in her testimony in the Galic case, Mr. Poparic. And then before she concluded her testimony, just to be perfectly clear about that, His Honour Judge El Mahdi even asked her why -- in fact, and that's in the Galic case at transcript page 3556, he asked her, Why, in fact, did you go out and she said she only went to the hospital to get medicine for her mother.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem regarding all of these incidents is that there is lots of information. One statement she said that she went to hospital to see her mother. I'm not denying that that statement may exist, too, but I don't know. I haven't come across it. I mean that she said that she was going to get medicine. So I based my assessment on her statement that she went to the hospital to visit her mother because her mother was in hospital, so there are several statements. Also, there are different statements about the time involved. So perhaps there are also different statements about the incidents themselves, but basically that doesn't really matter. The important thing is when the incident happened. Regardless --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Poparic, are you saying that when you prepared your analysis about this incident, you didn't review the witness's testimony in the Galic case? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I'm saying. I read the part where she spoke about the incident itself. Perhaps I missed that detail, that finesse, whether she was carrying medicine or whether she was going to get medicine because I thought that wasn't important. I thought that what was important was that she was going to the hospital and the time when she was on the bridge. That is the most important thing in relation to this incident. So all of these estimates can remain regardless of whether she went to the hospital to get medicine or whether she went to visit her mother. I don't see that that has anything to do with the incident itself. The only thing that is important is --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Poparic, I'd submit to you it has everything to do with your estimate as to the time at which this evidence -- this incident took place. You said -- I'll tell you what you said in your report. You said, at paragraph 81, halfway through the paragraph, Sanija Dzevlan went to visit her mother in the hospital at Dobrinja after lunch at around 1500 hours. It could have taken her about five minutes to cover the distance between her flat and the Dobrinja hospital by bicycle. It is common knowledge that hospitals normally allow visitors from 1400, 2.00 p.m., to 1600, 4 p.m., and that would usually be prolonged by an extra 15 minutes or so. Sanija Dzevlan would have kept an eye on the visibility outdoors and chosen the right time to leave so that she would not have to cycle in the dark. It's twilight on 6 January at 4.30 in the Sarajevo, but there is sufficient visibility to ride a bicycle. And you even go on. You say she was aware of the hospital's visiting hours and knew what time it was when she left the hospital after the visiting hours ended. So, Mr. Poparic, it's not me who is finessing the evidence, I would suggest it's you who is finessing the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that that is indispensable in order to establish the time. She said she went to the hospital, so it's based on the premise that she said she was going to the hospital to see her mother. I repeat once again that all of this fits into this period from 15- to 1630 hours. The question is only whether it was 15 minutes or half an hour earlier or later, things like that. I never said that the incident was exactly at 1630 hours or exactly at 1500 hours. I'm saying in that period. So that's why we gave these images in terms of visibility. At any rate, in that period of time in Sarajevo it's already dusk.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your premise is based on something wrong. She never said she was going to visit her mother at the hospital. She never said she stayed at the hospital. In fact, she told Judge El Mahdi in the Galic case she only went to the hospital to get medicine for her mother. Your premise and your summary of the evidence is incorrect, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that there is part of her statements where she says that she went to see her mother in hospital, and I based my assumption on that, that she was going to the hospital to visit her mother. But again I'm saying that is totally irrelevant. It's just the time that is important. If it's not 1630 then it was 1600 hours. It's in these findings. And we are not saying exactly that it was at 1630 hours, we are just giving a time range and we are analysing visibility in that period. It is totally irrelevant whether she was going to get medicine or -- or whether she had visited her mother. It's just -- how do I put this. It's just this half hour. At that time it's already dusk in Sarajevo so there is less visibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll move on. I suggested to you that you weren't summarising the evidence completely as well. And when I say that I mean you left out relevant material. And I'm going to give you an example: It's about the tank that you spoke about in your testimony at transcript page 38959 to 38960. You said that Mrs. Ramiza Kundo -- this is in relation to scheduled incident F5. You said that Mrs. Ramiza Kundo had said that there was a tank near a church on Brijesce Brdo and a military observer named Brennskag had said that as well. And you also referred to this tank in your report at paragraph 71. Now, what you didn't say in both your testimony and your report is that Mrs. Kundo actually testified that she didn't even know what year the tank was there. Could have been 1993 or could have been 1994. That's relevant, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Kundo, the tank is totally irrelevant for this incident. The fact is that she did say that there was a tank there and she also said that she never heard it fire and so on. But we did not quote that because we thought that that had nothing to do with this incident. The only thing that was said was that there were -- there were some military forces there at Brijesce Brdo. That's the only thing that was said in that sense, that there were members of the BH Army, I mean at Brijesce Brdo, and the tank has no direct link to the incident itself. And that's why we thought that we didn't have to go into all these details regarding the tank. Also, I mean, well, statements are different. Now, dealing with the tank, I don't see why we would do that in relation to this incident. The tank has nothing to do with this incident. It just shows that in that area, there were some forces of the BH Army. That is the point, why the tank was mentioned, but not in terms of firing. I mean when it was there, we didn't deal with that when it was there and whether the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not understand the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is only logical when you see the configuration of the train terrain.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The interpreters, and it's probably my fault, didn't understand the end of your sentence that finished with "... we didn't deal with that when it was there and whether the --" Could you finish the sentence for us and I apologise if I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The tank is totally irrelevant regarding this incident. We just mentioned it, I mean, as a fact that is being mentioned. I mean that there was a tank on this hill and that indicates that in that area there were members of the BH Army. It was only for that purpose, whether it fired or not, Mrs. Kundo said that she never heard it fire, and so on and so forth. That's a fact. But it's totally irrelevant regarding this incident, in our view.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you also think it was irrelevant that Mrs. Kundo said that the tank was only there on that site for about seven days, sometime within the two year period?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not for us to say when this happened. We just mentioned that there was a tank there. Now, when this happened, we could not investigate that period, when it was there. I hope that it was stated somewhere during this trial. It's not for us to establish how the tank was there. It's for us to deal with the incident. And if some evidence was adduced earlier, then that can be used, but we cannot present this kind of evidence and we did not deal with that and that was not the subject of our expertise, the tank I mean. So this is just a fact that we came across in the materials involved and we mentioned that. Evidence was probably presented through these proceedings; right? If that is useful for us, it wasn't useful at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Poparic, if you summarise evidence, it's important to do it as fully as possible and to avoid any risk of misleading the parties or anyone who is going to be listening to those summarise, don't you think?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that I mischaracterised it at all. She said it was a tank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. What objection at all, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the distinguished Madam Edgerton is lecturing the witness and telling him what he is supposed to do and how he's supposed to do it. She is supposed to establish what it is that he did do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Objection overruled. Yes, please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd like repeat the answer you just gave before Dr. Karadzic's intervention. I'm not sure we caught that.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we summarised, we summarised part of Ramiza Kundo's statement. She stated that there was a tank there. And we did not convey each and every detail because then it wouldn't have been a summary. A summary is something that is presented in brief. So the tank itself does not really matter with regard to this incident and that's why we thought that this didn't have to be looked into. Nobody said that the tank had fired and that she was perhaps injured from an explosion or something, so that's why I think it was not important at all to present each and every detail. It was only mentioned in the sense that she had said that there was a tank there. Namely, that there was a BH Army presence there. I mean, we did not have more material than that, or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Then in any case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Poparic, you said that the existence of tank is totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Totally irrelevant in the sense of assessing this incident. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why do you mention it at all in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we just mention it because Ramiza Kundo said there was a tank there. In our view if there was a tank there, then that means that they were on this hill Brijesce Brdo, that there were members of the BH Army, and that is the only thing that has to do with the tank and us. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it's relevant. It's relevant or irrelevant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the incident, irrelevant. We never said that Mrs. Ramiza Kundo was injured due to a shell being fired from the tank or something like that. It's relevant from the point of view that it may be considered that there were members of the BH Army on that hill, only in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, continue, Ms. Edgerton, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In any case, whether or not there was a tank there, that wouldn't give -- a tank there at whatever time, that doesn't mean you could snipe at civilians engaged in civilian activities, does it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think next I'd like to talk about some of your methodology. Now, you in your report referred to site visits to Sarajevo in September 2010 and May 2011, and you told my colleagues when they interviewed you on my behalf before your testimony in chief that this first visit was a three-day visit; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct. We left on Thursday morning and returned on Saturday. I think that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that was together with Mrs. Subotic and the object of that --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The object of that visit was to help the Defence for the cross-examination of the OTP witnesses. Have I accurately put to you what you told my colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only to help the Defence but for us to see what the site looked like and basically, well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you told my colleagues that the second visit in May 2011 was with Mr. Sladojevic to help prepare for the Trial Chamber's site visit; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not to help prepare for the Trial Chamber but to help Mr. Sladojevic because he wanted to familiarise himself with these places beforehand and we helped him in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you say, "We helped him," that kind of leads me to my next question. When you went with my colleagues or when you met with my colleagues, they asked you how you were able to find the correct locations to visit, and you said, you told them, you did that in two ways: The Defence provided a local person who lived there and had knowledge of the locations, and you had the case file documents; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you couldn't tell my colleagues the name of that local person?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could tell them but they didn't ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Could you tell us who he was?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can but maybe it would be a good idea to do it in closed session. I don't know whether that person would want this to be heard. If possible, closed session, just for a second so that I tell you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this individual, did he have or get knowledge of the locations because he'd been in the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He knew it because he was a member, he was very familiar with the area, he was born there, he lived there, so he didn't have any problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So my question was whether he had acquired his knowledge of the locations to visit because he'd been in the Bosnian Serb army, and I take it your answer is yes; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amongst other things, yes. That would be the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when that individual, during his service with the Bosnian Serb army, was that as a member of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I understood you was whether I was a member, or was it perhaps that you were asking me that person was a member? What was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct. I was asking you whether that person acquired his knowledge or during his service with the Bosnian Serb army was a member of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I assume that he acquired some of that information in the course of his service there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Did he get that knowledge because he had been a sniper?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did he get that knowledge because he had manned a mortar or artillery positions?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that he was a member of a tank crew, as far as I could understand from conversations with him; however, we did not mention his specific position during the war but, yes, he was a member.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So his job was to take you to locations where his forces, people he served with, are alleged to have shot the victims; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, his task was to help us to get to the location which was given in the indictment as the place from which fire was opened in one of the specific incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is yes, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you're talking about the places that are referred in the indictment. He was supposed to help us to get to the locations which are alleged in the indictment as the places from which fire was opened on the citizens of Sarajevo, and all that according to the indictment. We were familiar with those places. However, it was hard to get to those places. His assistance consisted primarily in showing us the best way to get to Spicasta Stijena, to Baba Stijena, and so on and so forth. The locations themselves were not a problem. The problem was how to get to them, how to choose the best way to get to those places. He was of great assistance to us with that. When it comes to the identification of those locations, we had materials that helped us. He did not say, This is where it was. There were materials that accompany the indictment and we realised that that was the place. His task was only to help us to get to those places. If you were ever there, you could see that the roads are narrow and curvy so he was of great assistance to us with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You told my colleagues when you met them and you were discussing these site visits, that you personally went to two locations for each sniping incident: The place where the victim was at the moment they were hit, and the place from which the shot might have originated. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. On several occasions, I went there on my own in situations when things needed to be clarified and we couldn't do it just based on the materials. On those occasions - I believe that I said that when your colleague was questioning me - I met with some victims, which is something that I didn't mention in my report because I thought that it wouldn't be fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you didn't tell my colleague this when he was questioning you, and you have never said, as you've just acknowledged, that you met with some victims in your report. As an expert --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's clarify. I said to your colleagues that I was there, that I met with the victims, and I explained the circumstances. It was not on my initiative. It was just the way things happened. They contacted me. And I did not enter that into the report because I didn't think it would be fair to convey a statement who contacted me with best of intentions. I didn't want to convey that because I didn't think it would be fair or human to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you meet with victims or survivors of any of the scheduled sniping incidents that are dealt with in your small arms report during any of your visits to the area?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with the victims. The people who I talked to were victims of the shelling at Markale II and the humanitarian aid. When it comes to sniping incidents, we had contacts with the person who helped a victim to be rescued. I believe that I said that and it is also contained in the report. That person told us where the exact location was. It was our assumption that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We will come there, all right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have contacts with victims from sniping incidents. I contacted the person who helped one of those victims to be transported to hospital and you will find that in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, when I asked you if it was correct that you personally went to two locations for each sniping incident, you said that you also went there on your own on several occasions when -- in situations when things needed to be clarified. Now in your evidence-in-chief, you mentioned an additional visit to the area in December 2012, and in relation to scheduled incident F4 you mentioned further visits to the area. Are we missing any other visits to the area than those on -- in December 2012 and in relation to scheduled incident F4? What else did you do that you haven't mentioned in your report?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in September 2012, I was on Brijesce Brdo, that's the location that you mentioned. I wanted to see once again whether there were any traces of the source that is mentioned in the documents. A witness stated that that source had dried up and is no longer active. I tried to see whether there were any natural traces pointing to the place where that source had been. On that occasion I couldn't see anything. I have some photos that I took. However, since I did not find anything, I never mentioned it in my report. In any case, the report had already been in by then. Subsequently, I went there just to put my mind at ease and to see for myself whether I was right the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I almost interrupted you and I apologise for that. You just said subsequently you went there. Does that mean that after September 2012 you went back to Brijesce Brdo again?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. In September 2012 I went there. My objective was to see the place again, it is a hill, there is a lot of grass, and I assumed that even if the source had dried up, it would have left some traces because if there is a source in an area, there are always traces of the erosion of the soil. But I could not see anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. So you went to visit this scheduled sniping incident sites in September 2011 -- pardon me, in September 2010, May 2011, September 2012, December 2012, and on a date we've not gotten into or several dates we have not gotten into with respect to sniping incident F4. Have you made any other visits to those sites that you haven't told us about in your testimony or your report?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for sniping incidents, no, but for some shelling incidents, I was there even before the official visit in 2010. I went to Spasenija Cana Babovic street, for example, for the following reason: In the documents, that place was described so that it could not fit within the contemporaneous map of Sarajevo. The names of the streets, the house numbers, everything was so confusing that it did not allow me to pinpoint the place of the shelling incident. So I went there to see what the street names were and what was what, and it was made very easy when I got there because there were a lot of reports with erroneous house numbers and street names, and based on those reports it was impossible to pinpoint the location with any precision. That's why I went there, to save time. And then in 2010, when we made the official visit, I just confirmed my initial findings. This is why I never mentioned that previous visit because it wasn't important. Our objective was primarily to see what the situation was precisely. That's why I didn't find it hard to get on a bus in the evening in Belgrade, I arrived in Sarajevo in the morning, I took stock of the situation, and went back home. I just wanted to make sure that my direction was not erroneous, that the analysis that we were going to make was not based on erroneous information. That was very important.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you went to the sniping incident locations, you told my colleagues that you didn't use a GPS to identify those locations even though you had GPS co-ordinates from Mr. van der Weijden's report; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, we did not use the system. We did not have to. I don't see a reason why I should have used the system. We had photos. We had exact addresses and everything else that we needed. That system would not have made a big difference. It would not have helped us a lot. We had the exact picture, we knew exactly what the situation was, and a GPS would have, for example, helped us in locating the position of the place but since that was not a problem we didn't really need the system at all. When you have photos and when you have all the other exact information, a GPS doesn't mean much. You can go to the place, you can measure the co-ordinates and you say -- you can say, These are the co-ordinates, but they don't mean anything. The GPS has been used for 25 years, and before it came into use the analyses were done in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if having a GPS doesn't actually mean much when you have photos -- let me ask you this another way. You would agree, though, wouldn't you, in cases of sniping, that differences of small metres can make a dramatic difference in assessing an angle of fire or an origin of fire? Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. In sniping incidents, a few metres do not mean much, and let me tell you why: A trajectory of a sniping round or sniping bullet is very straight, very horizontal. The ordinate is very low. Several metres do not mean much to us, if we do not have precise information about the nature of the hit, or rather, the nature of the wound. In none of the cases we had that. So the precision which is measured in terms of 1 or 2 metres even if we had a GPS system we wouldn't know where the bullet had come from. It could be 2 metres to one side or the other. And the possibility of the error is the same with or without a GPS because we did not have the precise information on the origin of the fire. It was just an assumption. Mr. Weijden, when he went there, he assumed that it was from there. He saw a trench and he assumed that the fire had come from that trench. It could have been some other trench. In concrete terms, let's try and remind ourselves of Spicasta Stijena. There were four trenches there that were used by the VRS. How can we know what trench the fire was opened from if we don't know the nature of the wound? That GPS system would not have been much of assistance in determining the origin of the fire in that incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. What about a laser rangefinder? Would that have been of assistance to you in the specific task that you had?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the conditions when we had information about the nature of the wound, but we didn't have any. So the laser beam would not have helped us a lot, because we did not know the exact origin of the fire because we could say it was -- the bullet was fired from 2 metres to the left or 2 metres to the right. We used the laser finder to measure, but that doesn't mean anything because we are not sure that the place was the exact place where the fire came from. So in all of these cases you can only talk about the approximate place from which the fire originated. There is another thing. We are talking about differences in the positions of one or the other side. When those differences are significant, then this can be of assistance, and this can help us to determine where fire had come from. But you have to know the exact position of fire in order for the laser rangefinder to give you the exact information in centimetres, and we can be off by 1 or 2 or even 3 metres because we don't know where the shooter was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the only equipment you had with you, as far as I understand it now, is a compass, and you didn't use that compass in your analysis of sniping incidents and I see from your evidence-in-chief that you must have had a camera because you told Dr. Karadzic that you took some of the pictures in your report; correct? That's all the equipment you had, a compass and a camera?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a camera, a measuring tape, a compass, a measuring tape is very important. Actually, it was a military compass, M-1, which we used to determine the axis. We used it but it was not of much use in sniping incidents because the place of the incident was located in terms of facility. We knew what the facility was and its exact position, so there were no disputes about that. The compass was of more use in the shelling incidents where we could see traces so we could determine the trajectory or the direction from which the shell had arrived. Here we have the exact position of the facility where the incident happened. We took measurements but those measurements were of no practical use to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to talk about some of these locations that you visited. For example, you talked in your testimony in chief about the white skyscrapers in Grbavica and that was in a number of places, transcript page 38994 and -996 to -998. Have you ever actually been up in those skyscrapers to the locations of the alleged sniper positions?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't go to those skyscrapers but we had a set of photos which were taken from those skyscrapers when the Trial Chamber in the Milosevic case visited the location. So we had a clear picture of what could be seen from those skyscrapers. We were aware of the concrete situation. That's why we thought that it was not necessary for us to go back there and take the exactly same photos.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So any analysis and calculations with respect to those skyscrapers as potential firing locations, you made on the basis of photographs; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The analysis was based on the height of the skyscrapers. That was what was important for the analysis. Even if we had visited the place, it would not have been of much use for our analysis. It could only help us to assure ourselves that it was possible to open fire from the skyscraper, but we don't know where the fire was opened for, from which floor, the 5th or the 10th. And then in our analysis, we used some bench-mark values, and since we are talking about the differences in the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska and the BiH army, and those are great, then the analysis of the angle of descent is very important. We had a case on the 27th of February when the traces showed that the bullet was fired at a large angle and it could not have been fired from the white skyscrapers. This is just an example of such an analysis. When we are talking about big differences then we can make our assessments with full reliability. When it comes to the skyscrapers, we don't know from which floor fire was opened.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How do you arrive at your bench-mark values?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know the distance between the skyscrapers; for example, the skyscrapers are involved in the incidents with the tram so we know the distance between the skyscrapers and the trams, we know the height of the skyscrapers, so the maximum height is the maximum angle which is about 10 degrees, if I remember it properly. And when you open fire from a building that is closer, the descent angle is much higher, there is drastic difference there. And based on that you can form your opinion as to whether fire was opened from a skyscraper or from somewhere else. Some positions were photographed there but we don't know on what floor, we do not deny that there were positions there. [Indiscernible] The white skyscrapers are across the street from the Marsal Tito barracks and I'm sure there were positions there facing the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you ever personally been inside the Metalka building to take a view of the area south down Franje Rackog Street?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what I was supposed to see. What do you mean? Do you mean that I went there to see the view of the street of Zmaja od Bosne? What was I supposed to see in the Metalka building?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you go into the Metalka building or not?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was next to the Metalka building in order to gauge the view down Franje Rackog Street. We also had a set of photographs taken in 2001, I think, when there was a visit concerning the Milosevic case. Those photographs were more useful because they were taken at a time when there was no vegetation, perhaps in November or so. There were no leaves, there was no foliage, so the view was better. At the time when we were there, all was green, so the view is more restricted than in the case when they were on their visit. In any case, even if we had gone to the Metalka building we wouldn't have been able to see anything, in order to determine whether there were positions there or not. It was 15 years after the war. The situation was changed completely. We could only see what the view is, which is perfectly clear to us, and we took it into account in all of our analyses. We did not deny that there was no visibility or anything of the sort. We simply conducted our analyses as if the visibility was 100 per cent, irrespective of the fact that there may have been a tree hampering the view.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, actually, when you told my colleagues that you had been to the victim location and the place from which the shot might have originated for each scheduled sniping location, that wasn't entirely correct, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did not establish that a victim was shot from the Metalka building or from the white skyscrapers. Our analyses indicate that no victim was hit from the Metalka building, save for the disputed case when a mother and her son became casualties, I think in November 1994. We cannot ascertain with any degree of certainty what happened, and where fire came from, given the contradictions that exist in our -- in the results of our findings, of our analyses, we did not establish, we did not find evidence that the Metalka was the source of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when we talk about locations, and you told my colleagues you went to the place from which each shot might have originated, I want to know where you went. You didn't go to the origin of fire that the victim --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I just finish my question? It seems like you didn't go to the origin of fire that the victims identified, you didn't go to the location the shooting -- the shooting position, the potential shooting position that Mr. van der Weijden identified. So where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to all those locations. If you have the Metalka in mind, we were next to it. We just didn't enter the building. And what was there to be gained by entering it? We don't know the exact place. Metalka is 50 metres in length. That is why we limited ourselves to such parts of the building that were visible, and from which we believed it was potentially possible to fire a bullet from any of those parts as provided in the analyses. The fact of entering the building would not have assisted our analysis. We took such facts into account where it was stated that the Metalka was the source of fire. And it was included in full in that part of the building which has a view of Franje Rackog Street, so it is not correct that we were not there. We just didn't go up the white skyscrapers, but we had the photographs taken from the high-rises in all directions, providing a clear indication of what could be seen and what could not be seen. We also didn't know which floor was used and nor did Mr. van der Weijden. However, it does not diminish the value of analyses at all. We did not deny it at any moment. We did not deny that something could be seen from the white skyscrapers or from the Metalka building. We took it into account. I even said that we did not limit ourselves to such positions where there were trees in the way. We believed we took into account that visibility was perfect, and on the basis of that we conducted our analyses.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in your report, at paragraph 14 (b), which is on page 36 in English, when you said, "We were unable to find concrete evidence of the presence of a sniper's hide in the Metalka building," that's not on the basis of any visit to the building itself, that's only on the basis of review of some material, some of your sources; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. It is understandable that 15 years down the road we cannot find traces. People live there now. In the documents we had at our disposal we did not find a piece of information which would indicate that someone saw a sniper position there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me add this: I do not claim that someone may not have said it but in the material we had, we did not come across it. If there is someone who said that, I will not dispute it, but we did not have such information, which doesn't mean that no one included such information. However, it is -- it was unavailable to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But it's misleading, isn't it, to present this information without any clarity as to whether that was from your own personal investigations of the scene or from a review of some second-hand information? It's misleading.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not. It cannot be misleading because we were there in 2010 which is 15 years later. Given the fact that the building was refurbished and people live there, how could that mislead anyone? It is reasonable to expect that we said so on the basis of the documents we had and not on the basis of an insight. It would be unreasonable to say that we were there in 2010 and to say, Yes, we were in the building but we didn't see a sniping position. Of course the building was renewed, people lived there, and there are no sniping positions there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you didn't say that to clarify your report because you thought it would be unreasonable?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We expected that everyone would understand that. I see nothing controversial in it, in order to put a particular stress on it. 2010, it's 15 years down the road, and I expect anyone reading it would understand that there were no such things then. As I explained we didn't find it because we couldn't have found it in 2010. If the building had caved in and had not been refurbished then it would have been logical to stress that, to say the building was not rebuilt, et cetera. In any case, Mr. van der Weijden didn't say either that he found snipers there. He couldn't have. He was there a few years before us, and even then there were no traces, nor could there have been any.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. But Mr. van der Weijden, Mr. Poparic, having gone to the building was able to say that there were possible shooting positions down Franje Rackog Street at all levels of the building, and that was at transcript page 7097 and you can't say that. The only evidence you have about possible shooting positions comes from you standing somewhere near the building at a location you've not identified for us yet.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You completely misinterpreted. We did not say anywhere that in the Metalka building there were such places from which fire could not be opened. Had we said that, then this activity of yours would have had a basis. What we said, as we analysed, was that from the Metalka building it was possible to open fire from the 1st, 2nd or 5th floor, we don't know that, but we know the extreme left and extreme right position. From those positions it was possible; that is to say, from any part of the Metalka building it was possible to open fire. We did not deny anything that Mr. van der Weijden said. We completely took it into account, as if each and every window had a sniping position from which fire was opened. That -- those were the conditions in which we carried out our analysis. I think that is clearly visible in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Just a few more questions about your sources. I think that it's fair to say now, having talked about this for a little while, that apart from some general references to other documents during your testimony in chief, and even today and during your cross by my colleague, it seems obvious that the documents you cited in your small arms report represent only a small part of everything you reviewed in its preparation?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, we went through much more of the material. In order to arrive at what you need, you need to go through very voluminous material, but we did not mention all of it. We only referred to such documents that we relied on, that were important to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And almost all of the material that you reviewed in connection with this report was material given to you by Dr. Karadzic's Defence - in fact, you told my colleagues it was a big pile of CDs full of material - and the only additional material you took steps to secure for yourself was what you downloaded off the ICTY website from the Galic and Dragomir Milosevic cases; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, it is right. We downloaded it from the Tribunal website. We downloaded some things. Since there was this technical possibility, we relied on it so as not to ask for everything from the Defence because it was a burden to them. So we relied on that, we relied on the material we located ourselves, and we used the photographs and footage made on the visit -- during the visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So otherwise you felt that the collection of material you had received from Dr. Karadzic's Defence counsel was pretty complete; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. We do not believe so. It is in the report. In the material, what is missing is a lot of documentation that has to do with injuries, with forensic evidence, court evidence. There is material missing but that was not part of the case file. It would have been useful if we had had it but it wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you take independent steps to go and get it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did. We asked Defence to see whether they can locate it but they couldn't. In some cases, they did find some documents but in others they did not. As far as I can see, Mr. van der Weijden did not have such information either so I supposed that there was no extra information in that regard. So he didn't use the forensic pathology documentation which may be crucial in order to ascertain exactly what happened. It is very important in a few cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let me ask you just a bit about that since you got on the topic. You told us in your evidence-in-chief that you consulted with a forensic medicine professor from the university, Dr. Jovan Dunjic, and that was according to what you said in regard to sniping incident F12. That's not in your report, is it, that consultation? You don't mention it anywhere in your report.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mention it in the report because based on the consultation, I did not base any of my assertions on it. We did not state anything explicitly. The professor himself told me that based on what he could see, he could agree with some of my assumptions, that it was more likely that it came from the left, but that he could only provide his final determination based on a forensic -- on the forensic analyses done at the time. It is completely unimportant because we did not decidedly say that it was so. I simply wanted, because we do not have that analysis, to have it for myself because I created my conclusions based on the photographs and the footage. I'm an engineer so I have an eye for the geometrical differences. I also went to see an expert, a professor, who could tell us, You were off completely, or, You may well be right. But that needs to be proven. And that was the answer we received. In terms of the photographs he said that, I would say your conclusions were correct. However, without a full analysis I can't say anything for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When did you go and consult with this Dr. Dunjic? Do you even remember the year?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime when we were drafting the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you don't have any notes of your consultation --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm trying not to interrupt you but, please, don't interrupt me. So you don't have any notes of your consultation with Dr. Dunjic?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I went to his office. We sat down for about two or two and a half hours. I showed him the material. It was in the stage where we were still working on the material. It was during the summer, perhaps July. I can't say exactly. In any case, I did not keep notes. It was an informal visit so that the two of us could meet to see if he could help me. We simply sat down and talked. I did not keep notes precisely because I did not cite it as a reference to the report. It was just an assistance to -- for me to have a calm conscience, clear conscience. I wanted to receive an opinion from an expert in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you consulted with any other forensic or legal or investigative or military or other experts when you were preparing this report that you haven't told us about?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you spoken with any of Dr. Karadzic's Defence witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Including Mr. Slobodan Tusevljak whose name you mentioned in your evidence-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Tusevljak? I don't know. I saw him for the first time during his testimony when I watched it. I don't even know what his position was. I was interested since an incident that we considered was discussed. But I don't know whether you see Mrs. Subotic as a witness but I did speak to her. We worked together.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you spoken with any snipers?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean snipers, from the VRS or in general?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's start with in general. Did you consult with any snipers, any trained snipers, in the preparation of this report?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the process of compiling the report, I did not, but I did have some conversations with sharp shooters in the course of my career. I was in frequent contact with professional sharp shooters who were engaged in such things throughout their career at firing ranges, training ranges, in the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. But that wasn't what I asked you. I asked you about the preparation of this report and you answered that question. Now, I want to go back to the material you received from Dr. Karadzic's Defence. You said that the only steps you took independently to inquire about additional documents was to direct your queries to Dr. Karadzic's Defence. You only asked them for what you thought might be missing; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know who else I could have asked anything. They were the only connection. I don't know who else I could have consulted on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. I want to just look at one of the documents that you referred to in preparing your report, and that's the military map that you cited as image 12, at page 42, and then you cite it again as image 49 and then again at image 52. And I don't want to call up a document just yet but that map - and I see you have your report open in front of you in the Serbian version with the images in it - was that map given to you by Dr. Karadzic's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was in the documents. Perhaps we misquoted and instead of the 14th it should have been the 12th Division. The first time you make that mistake you just carry it on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'd actually like to look at the whole map which is P1764 for a minute, please, and once it's called up just to zoom in on the top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't follow. You don't have e-court? It's not -- it's coming. Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Our e-court isn't displaying the map yet, but maybe it's still loading.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's a big file, so it takes a moment and time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I don't have e-court at all, the whole morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, we haven't used it. Probably it's time to take a break then. So I'll ask the technician to take a look at it. Yes, Ms. Edgerton, it's coming but you haven't -- you're not seeing that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There is no point if Dr. Karadzic can't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, then we shall take a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Karadzic, your e-court is now working?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Excellency. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Poparic, you should see a part of the military map that you took the cut-outs in your report from, P1764, on the screen in front of you. Now, if you look at the top left-hand corner of this map, you see that the operative date is March 1st to 14 September 1995; right? Maybe we could zoom it in a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So nowhere in your report did you point that out, did you? Instead, you used this map from 1995 as evidence of the positions of the front lines in relation to an incident dated September 1993 in Hrasno and another one dated November 1993 in Brijesce Brdo?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would not agree that I never said that. I quoted it in the footnote, which document was used, that is. I mean, well, as far as the relevance of this map is concerned, I did bear in mind that the dates differed, and then I tried to see in the documents whether there were some documents that would indicate that the situation on the ground was different at the time of the incident, and I did not find any such documents. As for Brijesce Brdo, I found some witness statements to the effect that the separation lines in that area were roughly the same, like on this map. The terrain itself shows -- shows, I mean -- well, that this map -- well, roughly depicts the situation as we did in the report because there are some natural obstacles.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You have, with respect, a tendency to give very long answers and I understand that you're trying to be helpful, but my time to do this is limited, so sometimes I may have to direct you a little bit more strongly than I have been. Mr. Poparic, you, in the footnote to this map, every time you used it, referred to it as something other than what it was. You didn't disclose that it was a map from 1995 and that's misleading, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think no. This map was introduced and what is written there is written there. If the date is the problem, 1995, I mean that's what is written there, that cannot be concealed by anyone. In the parts that we used that was the situation. In Ozrenska Street we accepted the situation from this map and the only thing that could have happened was that the BH Army units were close her to Ozrenska, not further down, that's for sure. Once you get to the ground, it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We will talk about Ozrenska Street when we talk about the incidents, but, Mr. Poparic, you've -- what you've said today shows that you've considered and deliberately omitted relevant information from your report repeatedly. You've developed premises based on incorrect information. Your sources, Mr. Poparic, are not transparent. You've not disclosed consultations and conversations that you had relative to this report in the report. All of that is misleading, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, absolutely not. This is a map that is evidence and I disagree, and I'm telling you that we did not do anything that would have changed the situation. We considered the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska to be where you claim they were, where that photograph was made, and we accept that. Also for Brijesce Brdo, we accept that the building from which it is claimed the fire came was in the territory of the VRS, just as this map shows, and I don't see what we used there that was not relevant. As for your assertion that I concealed some consultations, I could not accept that because if I talked to Professor Dunjic, I talked personally to check some of my own observations. I did not insist that this was Mr. Dunjic's opinion. He will be here and you can ask him. As for consultations about the visit, I mean as for talking to the witness, I mean, I did not even include that in the report so I would not accept --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, I'm sorry, I want to go back before you go on very far to something you've just said. You've just said Mr. Dunjic will be here and you can ask him, but I asked you earlier whether or not you had spoken with Defence witnesses and you said no. Is Mr. Dunjic a Defence witness that you spoke with?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I found out about that only later. I omitted that, sorry. Well, don't -- I mean I talked to Mr. Dunjic as a professor and as a forensic medicine expert. That's how I talked to him. I did not talk to him about his testimony and I don't know what he's going to testify about. That's the point. So for me at the point in time when I talked to him he was not a Defence witness. He was a professor and a forensic medicine expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. I'd like to go on to some of the scheduled incidents you discussed in your testimony and report and I'd like to begin with one that happened on the 1st of July, 1993, that's the killing of Munira Zametica as she was trying to get water from the Dobrinja River. And you discuss it at pages 48 to 52 of your report, in English, and paragraphs 39 to 52. Now, you told the Trial Chamber that we had no reliable information about the time of this incident, and between your report and your testimony, as I understand your position on this, you discarded the evidence of an eyewitness and the victim's daughter who testified before this Tribunal, which placed the time of the incident between 2.00 and 3.00 on the one hand and 2.00 and 2.30 on the other, and you discarded a hospital death certificate setting out Mrs. Zametica's time of death at 4.00 p.m., and instead you told the Court that the police had registered the incident between 7.00 and 7.30, and a witness mentioned that she and the victim had set out for the river just before night fall. So I understand your position correctly, do I? That's kind of a yes-or-no answer.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you just a yes or a no answer. I took all the times into account. But my assumption is on the basis of everything that it is more probable that it was at dusk, and I can explain why, but all the times were looked at and nothing was concealed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. But you didn't tell the Judges in your report or in your testimony that the very same witness who mentioned that she and the victim had set out for the river before night fall, that's Mrs. Sahinovic, was shown the police report, and she specifically -- she specifically in her testimony before the Judges in the Galic case, said that the time on the document was incorrect and that she and the victim had gone to the river in mid-afternoon. And she said that at Galic transcript page 3440. You omitted that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't mention that detail but I did say that during her testimony she said that she went to fetch water when night was supposed to fall. That was rather descriptive, this testimony. And then at the intervention of the Prosecutor, she corrected that assertion and she gave this time, between 2.30 and 3.30, so that's not being contested, and I did not conceal that, that Mrs. Sahinovic said that she was there at that time. But in her statement, both is stated, so that's a fact. And this other thing she said, that when night would fall, I mean that coincides with what the police report says. So I did not base the report on that, rather -- actually these are only facts that were before me. I said that I analysed both cases which is important. And now which time exactly, I wouldn't want to go into all of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just believe that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More accurate --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You agree that you didn't mention in your report the fact that Sadija Sahinovic corrected the information in the police report that she specifically said that it was incorrect. You didn't mention her correction at all. And for the record that police report the witness referred to in his own report is D672.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that I didn't mention that but I did mention that she corrected her statement that she set out as night was supposed to fall so that coincides with that time so I did not confirm that fact, but I did not conceal that she had said both and that she said this time. So she corrected her time and I did not conceal that. You cannot say that I concealed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What I'm saying is, again, you omitted relevant information. The specific document you choose to rely on to support your contention that this incident took place between 7.00 and 7.30 was corrected by the witness on the witness stand.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree, because she corrected her testimony in the courtroom when namely that she had set out that when it was supposed to be night-time and she corrected it, and I don't see any significant difference there, and later on she denied that particular time of 19- to 1930 hours, and she said that it's not correct that she went out to get water as night was supposed to fall. So there is no problem in terms of me concealing something.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in regard to this incident, you talked about the Orthodox Church at Bijeljina in your testimony, and you said that you were in the church tower, and about that you said you would personally never put a sniper there in the church tower for a couple of reasons, and that was at transcript page 38953. First of all, you said the space is very little in the tower, it's insufficient to secure the place, and the place was too exposed. That's your personal opinion; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my personal opinion, yes. Otherwise I did not have any information as to what the church tower looked like at the time and whether there had been a sniper positioned there but we conducted this analysis as if there had been a sniper there in that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you didn't receive in all the material that you received from Dr. Karadzic's Defence counsel or his Defence team, you haven't received any information that would go to show that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had a sniper in the church tower at Veljine?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have such information, but that is why we did not rule out that possibility. So we looked at all of that as if there had been a firing position there and that it had been fired from, and that is the only thing that matters for this incident, and I assumed that through other evidence this will be either confirmed or denied.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, interpreters didn't catch your answer in full.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did catch the entire answer but with great difficulty. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Appreciate it. Mr. Poparic, could you kindly come closer to the microphone, so that the interpreters can hear you better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter number 25108, please? Thank you. Could you make the B/C/S -- enlarge the B/C/S original a little bit, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, this is a report from the intelligence organ of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 5th Motorised Brigade, 1st Motorised Battalion, and it's dated 2 October 1993 and that's three months after this incident. If we go down to the bottom of page 1 in B/C/S and the last sentence on the -- your indulgence for a moment -- I've omitted to mark the reference in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it's at the top of page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, last sentence in the bottom of page 1 in English and we stay on page 1 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This report says that from Dobrinja 4 towards the church at Veljine the enemy has made a connection trench, and in the area behind the garage a bunker was built. Do you see it, Mr. Poparic? It's about in your language almost halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see it. Could you please zoom in a bit? I can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, that's the wrong portion. Move up to where you see the words Dobrinja 4, please. Thank you. So the enemies made a connection trench and in the area behind the garage a bunker was built from which they opened fire only at night. And further it says -- further it says the enemy uses the church at Veljine exclusively as an observation post. According to our information till now there are six observers per shift. The observers are armed with snipers and one anti-aircraft machine-gun which is in a well-fortified nest in the church, and from the church fire is rarely opened and when it's opened a sniper with a silencer is used. So --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is evidence which tends to confirm that Sarajevo Romanija Corps firing position at the church was operative and that sniper rifles were used from that location. So based on this contemporaneous military document, it looks like your personal opinion as to where you might put a sniper is actually unreliable, because this is evidence that, one, was located in the Orthodox Church tower.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this document refutes my opinion. I think it confirms it, as a matter of fact. It is stated here that at the church tower there was an observation post, an observation post, which is only logical because it's high up and an observation post is used as a hidden place from which one can observe the activities of the other side. I mean, this is a BH Army source, and they can assume that they had snipers, but they say themselves, I mean, that it is rarely used for opening fire. There is something illogical here. It says here, armed with snipers and a PAM that is in a well-fortified nest in the church. A PAM is an anti-aircraft machine-gun. It's not a sniper. And they say that fire was opened seldom. That means it wasn't really opened. So this information about the weapons, I mean, about these observers on the church tower, it is like my assumption, and this is now their assumption, but I see here that they are not saying when they fired and -- I mean an observer, as a person who is supposed to be hidden, of course, should be armed --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, does it confirm your point or not? You said, when you first looked at this document, it confirms it, and what are you trying to say now? It doesn't?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This confirms that this was not a typical sniper position but it was an observation post rather, which according to the impression that I had at this church was quite possible. It says here that these observers were armed. All observers are armed, right? But an observer by definition does not use his position for opening fire but only for observing. That's why he's called an observer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, you actually have already told my colleague that you have never worked as a sniper and it's obvious that you have no tactical know-how relating to sniper deployment or operations other than the conversations you've had in the past over the course of your career; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. I'm an officer. You shouldn't forget that. I had been trained as officer. I completed the necessary school. I know what the sniper's role is, what fighter's role is. An observer is always posted in a forward post which is risky and he doesn't open fire unless absolutely necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll get into that when we go into other scheduled incidents. I want to draw your attention to something that you said in your report at page 49 of the English, paragraph 42. You concluded that because the eyewitness Mrs. Sahinovic saw bullets hitting the water which prevented any rescue of Mrs. Zametica but didn't hear any gunfire, either her hearing was impaired or the weapon used had a silencer. So if you read this document, it looks like Mrs. Sahinovic's hearing on the 1st of July, 1993, was working perfectly fine. Couldn't that have been the case?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a possibility, but it cannot be claimed for a fact that that was what really transpired. We don't know what Mrs. Sahinovic's hearing was, what she heard either. This is just an assumption of the circumstances. If it was a silencer, that doesn't mean that fire had to be opened from the church. There is not enough evidence to corroborate that. This is just one of the options.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this as a Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6360, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You have -- you told my colleague -- never served in combat; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You never served in the Bosnian army; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You were never in Sarajevo during the conflict, let alone Dobrinja; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you have actually no idea how forces defending Dobrinja were organised on July 1st 1993 other than what you might have read; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. However, I had an occasion to see statements provided by the commander of the Dobrinja Brigade; therefore, I know how it was organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, that's what I asked you. I said you have no idea how they were organised other than what you might have read. You've not spoken yourself to any of the local commanders; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Actually, the answer is yes. I never did. I didn't speak to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you haven't been able to identify any of the soldiers who suddenly appeared and opened fire from the bridge in the direction of the church that Mrs. Sahinovic referred to?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, of course not. Nobody ever identified them so I couldn't do it either.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you mean for us to infer that they were on duty on the bridge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that they were armed, actually those detail here which does not tally with the description of the events.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, you're not answering my question. Do you mean for us to infer that they were on duty on the bridge? Is that why you wrote about that in your report?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't really matter. Not about that but about the fact that they were close by and that they opened fire from the bridge, which means that there was an opening on the bridge from which they could open fire, given the fact that there were sandbags on the bridge, and that's the point. Maybe you want me to describe how the defence was organised. I believe that General Vahid Karavelic spoke about the organisation of the defence. They had the first, they had the forward defence line, the --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
