utterances.text: -- because General Karavelic spoke about that under oath in front of another Trial Chamber in this building. I want to know what you know.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. So when you talked in your report about these soldiers - and that's at paragraphs 45, 46 and 47 of English page 50 - and said that the soldiers were on duty, that was only on the basis of what you read from what other witnesses might have given evidence about; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I said that they had probably been on duty because they were armed. Whether they were deployed there or somewhere nearby it's neither here nor there, but since they had weapons and since they opened fire it's only logical that they were on duty. We heard several testimonies to the effect that the soldiers would leave the weapons behind when they were sent home.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't want you to talk about what the other testimonies might have said in your answer. What you've said effectively is that your assertions that they were on duty were actually nothing but guess-work. You've never been in Dobrinja, you don't know how the forces were organised, you haven't spoken to the commanders, you don't even know who the soldiers were, so your conclusion that they were on duty is a leap of logic that has no foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I don't think Ms. Edgerton is being fair to the witness when she tells him, I don't want you to talk about what the other testimonies might have said in your answer. If he has information from whatever source he's entitled to give it as part of his answer. She can't restrict that. In fact, she's been criticising him for not taking into account testimony which contradicted an earlier report. So you can't preface a question by that, and I think it gives the witness a misleading impression that he's not able to make a complete answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I think he's trying to answer that his conclusion was based upon other evidences, other witnesses' testimony. But, Mr. Poparic, could you make your answer a bit simpler?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best. My basic conclusion based on which I thought that they were on duty is that they were armed. Second of all, I came across statements by several persons who were members of the BiH army who said that they had left their arms behind in the units when they were sent home. And based on that, I assumed that they were on duty because they were armed. In wartime it can happen that a soldier takes weapons home. That's a fact. However, I know that they claim that they didn't have enough weapons and that they left weapons behind when they were sent home and they would go home unarmed. And the fact is that those soldiers opened fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions briefly before we leave this incident. Have you gone to the specific incident location where this witness was at the time she was shot, between 2.00 and 3.00 p.m. on any date at all?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the witness's answer. Could the witness be asked to speak clearly into the microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say anything else after having said yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said, "Yes, I did."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us when that was, because it's not in your report?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in September 2010, either on the 17th or the 18th, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask which witness this refers to on line 15 on page 47?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 50 of Mr. Poparic's report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you take any photographs at that moment?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I did take photos. However, they would have been little use of those photos because a new building has sprung up in front of the church. The photo that may be of use was taken by the OTP. In that photo you can see the church from a position somewhere below the bridge, and I believe that zoom was used. We did not report on that. I suppose it may have been useful if we did report on that. In any case, one can see the church from the place where that photo was taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, in paragraph 50 of your report, you said that if the incident took place between 2.00 and 3.00 p.m., the sun made a shadow in the place where Munira Zametica was shot. Now you've just said you were at that location, the precise location that -- where she was when the bullet hit her, and you took photographs. Where are the photographs?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to clarify something. I was there and the position of the sun is such that it creates a shadow. Even if I had taken a photo at that time it would not have been useful because there was a row of sandbags 2 metres high which cast an additional shadow. Second of all, I was in a place below the bridge at -- more or less where she was, but I was not in the place where she was hit because she was in the riverbed. The riverbed is concrete and at a high slant. The only thing that was never said is this: How did people descend into the river? There must have been a staircase there. We don't know how they were -- it was made, whether people were sheltered by the staircase or not. I could not --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't ask you anything about the staircase. We are talking about the photographs. So my question is, and I'm trying to find the source to support the evidence you set out in paragraph 50 of your report. My question is: Did you take photographs of the area between 2.00 and 3.00 p.m. so we can see whether the sun made a shadow in the place where Mrs. Zametica was shot? Now, as I understand your answer now, it's no, you didn't take photographs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I did not take photos. Those photos would not have been relevant because the 2-metre high sandbag wall was not there, and at the time it made a shadow, and as for the position of the sun and the shade, it's easily checked if you look at the map of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. And you weren't in Dobrinja during the war. You've said that. You weren't at this location during the war. So actually you don't know what kind of shadow the sandbags would have made, if at all, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with war. The position of the sun and its shadow are astronomic terms and that can be checked at any moment. Look at a map orientation, weather conditions, time, and everybody will understand what the position of the sun was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how the sandbags may or may not have been stacked, what height, what depth, where along the bridge they were located has nothing to do with that. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't think the interpreters caught your answer. The sentence seems incomplete because I read here, "According to statements."

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position of the sandbags was such that they were distributed on both sides of the bridge and they were 2 metres high, and if the sun came from that side, they had to made a shadow on the opposite side. And if those sandbags had not been there, the shadow would not be -- would not have been as big. It's easily proven by simple geometry. A photo taken in 2010 would have been pointless because those sandbags were not there and the situation was completely different. And this is the main reason why we didn't take any photos at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. I'd like to go to another part of Sarajevo now and incident F17 which took place in Sedrenik, and you deal with this incident at paragraphs 198 to 206 of your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before going further, what's the date of this incident, F3, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 1st of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not 11?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this incident, I'd like to look at a couple of the documents you cited as your sources. You said, in paragraph 199, that no on-site investigation into this incident was conducted due to combat operations. So by that you mean combat between the warring factions; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look at one of your sources, 65 ter 10367, which you cite in footnote 348. And this is a police report on the incident. The English translation should be coming. Paragraph 3 of this document says: "Due to firing from the aggressors' positions at the place where Tarik Zunic was wounded, we could not conduct an on-site investigation." So the document, on its face, says absolutely nothing about combat, does it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document says due to fire from aggressors' positions, there are, however, UNPROFOR documents that speak about ongoing fighting. There is a document which says that the Egyptian Battalion got involved in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does not rule out fighting at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, I'm just asking you about this document for the moment and we are going to come to the UNPROFOR document. Is it correct that this document says absolutely nothing about combat?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it says here that there was fire from the aggressors' positions, which does not rule out the possibility that fire was returned. They could not approach because of the fire which was opened from the aggressors' positions. This does not rule out the possibility that fire was returned, that fire was opened against those aggressors's positions but maybe that was done from another position.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But that's an assumption that you've made; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I'm just saying how things would be interpreted, that this does not rule out different possibilities -- does not rule out a different possibility because he explains in the report why they didn't immediately rescue the boy because of the fire. It is only logical that the BH Army did not open fire on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So that is actually the only document that you footnote to paragraph 199, which says due to combat operations no on-site investigation was conducted. So just leaving the UNPROFOR document aside for the moment, this document, on its face, doesn't support your assertion in paragraph 199, does it? Because it doesn't say anything about combat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On what basis and what objection do you have, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to the fact that the footnote in paragraph 199 is not cited in order to prove whether there was combat going on or not. It is cited in order to prove the nature of the wound. We received information that the boy was slightly wounded through the palm of his hand. This is why this document is cited. This is not to prove that there was combat going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we move on?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As this is one of the witness's sources, could I have this as Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6361, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could we go over to the UNPROFOR report that you just talked about, it's P1619 and it's cited in footnote 349 to paragraph 200. You say that the UNPROFOR document from this day confirms claims that the document that we've just looked at confirms claims from this document that ongoing combat operations, as it states, there was much fighting going on in the area. So what you cite to is paragraph 4(c) of this UNPROFOR document. And that's at page 2 in B/C/S and in English, although in English paragraph 4(c) begins at the bottom of page 1. So what you do is you cite to the report of eight explosions, seven machine-gun bursts and 93 rounds of small arms fire. And do you see -- could we go over to the next page in English? Thank you. Do you see the asterisk after the mention of 93 rounds of small arms fire? And the asterisk then at the end of this table of small arms violations says, see paragraph 3(a). Do you see that asterisk? Mr. Poparic, do you see the asterisk on the table that you cite to?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are four. I don't know which one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The asterisk is a small star shape symbol and it appears in this document after the mention of 93 -- the reference to 93 rounds of small arms fire. Do you see that? It's the little star shaped symbol and it's at the top middle of the page that's in front of you on the screen. My colleague has put the cursor right beside it so you can see the asterisk.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That asterisk --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- tells us to refer to paragraph 3(a) of the same document. So I'd like to do that and go back over to page 1, please, in both versions. Now, paragraph 3(a) says, "While assisting casualties reported at paragraphs 8," and that - I'm sure you would agree, we can check it if you don't - includes Mr. Zunic, "UNMOs came under occasional small arms fire. Number of rounds unknown but origin of fire assessed at being Sharpstone." All right? So that gunfire you cited to is assessed as coming from Sharpstone by the UNMOs. And I'd like to go down to paragraph 3(b), which says: "As a result of coming under fire while assisting sniper casualties, the UNPROFOR EgyptBat anti-sniping team returned fire on Bosnian Serb army positions at Sharpstone. Following this, the UNMO Vogosca team received a telephone call from the commander of the Radava Battalion Vogosca Brigade saying that if the EgyptBat APC in his target practice area wasn't moved within half an hour, it would be fired upon." So this document also says nothing about combat, does it? What it reports is direct targeting of the rescue of wounded civilians by SRK forces from Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree that it doesn't mention any combat. One can see here that fire was returned from the Egyptian APC. If there is no information on any combat with the ABiH, there is information on combat with members of the Egyptian Battalion. There was an exchange of fire. In addition to what was stated there, we indicated that there was a lot of firing, which is confirmed by the report. We saw all of the activities concerning the incident. In our view, such activity does not entail individual sniper fire at the boy. It seems the boy was hit in an exchange of fire opened in a general area from machine-guns, infantry weapons, and what not. So there is information on the opening of fire. In our view, the boy, under such circumstances, could not have been an isolated target intentionally targeted by a sniper. That is what was concluded on the basis of those activities. This confirms that there was combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When I asked you at the beginning of our discussion about this incident whether you meant combat between the warring factions, in reference to your report, you said yes. So now you are changing your evidence to suit your -- the point you're trying to make, aren't you? Because now you're talking about combat between UNPROFOR and the SRK. So what you're saying is victim here Tarik Zunic was wounded in cross-fire between UNPROFOR and the SRK? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I say that there was an exchange of fire, you said that there was no specific evidence that there was. There was an exchange of fire which is indicated in the document. Of course, when there is an exchange of fire, someone may get caught in cross-fire between the parties engaged. It is only logical. I don't know, though, why it is not specifically addressed here. We see that there was a fierce exchange of fire as confirmed to me by the man who was present. He said that there was fierce combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's just talk about that man for a minute. Now, you went to this street, Sedrenik Street, at some point in your site visits, I understand. You didn't speak with the victim at that time, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So even though his family home was about four houses away from the scene of the incident, you didn't go there and ask to be taken to the exact incident location, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think that's an unfair question. Had he done that he would have been in violation of our protocols concerning contacts with Prosecution witnesses. He's not allowed to do that. So to criticise him for not doing that is unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd just like to move on actually, Your Honours, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you went to the area, you didn't go to the house immediately behind the location where Tarik Zunic was shot, the house with the red fence that he identified in his evidence in the Dragomir Milosevic case, did you? You didn't go there to ask about the incident location.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was our intention to go in front of the house because we had the photographs at our disposal which he had marked. We identified the house and we were approached at that moment by a man who resides in the next house.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's just talk about how you identified the house for a minute. Could we have a look at -- your indulgence for a moment -- P451 in this case, please. Thank you. Now, in his testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case, the victim marked the X on this location on the street in front of the house where he was shot. So did you go to the house behind that red fence that we see on the right-hand side of this photo?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not. We had no authority to go into people's homes. But we were on location. It was the first location that we visited.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you were with members of the police forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, during that site visit in September, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but before the tour we had a meeting with the SIPA director, the organisation in charge of the visit, and we agreed on the terms of the visit. We had no authority to go into people's homes. We could talk to people, and in the course of such conversations, we were not supposed to introduce ourselves as representatives of Defence. We were told for security reasons to introduce ourselves as a team which has a connection with The Hague Tribunal. That was the arrangement with the SIPA director and that is how we approached it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine and that's fair enough. So without going into somebody's home, your evidence is you didn't ask to go knock on the door, you didn't ask the police to knock on the door of this specific house immediately in front of the location where the boy has marked he was shot?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So when you met my colleagues on the 27th of May, you told them about this man and woman who you spoke with from a house down the street. Who else was present at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Subotic was, then the man who served as our escort, there were policemen. Everyone was there. I can explain the circumstances. It wasn't our plan to visit it. Why didn't we go there? Because we recognised the location.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like you to listen to my questions actually. Did you record the names of this man and woman and their contact details?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not. The man offered his services. However, I abided by the agreement we had with the SIPA director and I did not introduce myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not supposed to reveal our identity, and that is why I did not want to take any information from him. It would have been unfair. In any case, I did not contact the man first. He approached us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So nobody took notes of the interview either? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is right. I believe I said so. He came to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, at this specific location, from this specific location where the victim marked he was shot, you then -- and you've confirmed it in your report -- you were able to see that Spicasta Stijena was visible from that site, and you confirmed it, if you want to double check, in paragraph 204; right? You took a view from that spot and you could see a clear line of sight to Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. One can see it from this position. However, as for the other position shown to us by the man, visibility is less. The first location has better visibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. Your indulgence for a moment, please. All right. I'd like to go on to another incident but stay in the area of Sedrenik, and that's scheduled sniping incident F2. You talked about this in paragraphs 31 to 38 of your report and that is at pages 45 to 48 of the English translation. Now, just before we get into some of the physical details, you said in your analysis of this incident that the victim who was shot was kneeling down with her back turned towards the house and her head was facing the street. And you footnoted this to her testimony in the Galic case. But -- and the footnote is to transcript page 4036. But, Mr. Poparic, in fact, there is no reference on that page or anywhere in her testimony that she was facing the street. She says, at lines 5 to 6 of that page, and she clarified at transcript pages 4042 and 4047, that she was facing spiky rock which is Spicasta Stijena at the moment she was shot.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it. If she was turned in the direction of Spicasta Stijena, it is understood that she was looking in that direction. The position itself was explained by Mr. Barry Hogan in the footage. One can clearly see her indicating where she was turned to. It corresponds to the description provided, although perhaps we did not convey it in as much detail, but that was her position. She was kneeling down with her back to the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that, or correcting that. So it's clear, when I read your report, that you've read the victim's witness statement, you've included that in one of your -- as one of your sources, her statement of 25 June 2001, so you would have read her evidence that the bullet hit the wall of the house behind her and the chipped cement -- and chipped the cement and the mark of that was still visible. You would have read that evidence. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. van der Weijden's report has the same evidence at page 22 and in particular page 23. He even has a photo of the preserved bullet strike. You didn't go to the specific location of the incident where you could see the preserved bullet strike mark, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The house had a part added on to, as you can see in Barry Hogan's footage from 2001. In all likelihood we wouldn't be able to find it. We didn't go to see where it was but we were in the area and that's where the photograph was made. We did not see the trace itself, though, and I don't know if it still exists.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you not ask to go see it? Because it would have been an ideal situation and an excellent opportunity from which you could analyse direction of fire, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't. It wouldn't. According to our information, that part is now fenced in. I think there is a garage there nowadays. It is no longer the same place. It doesn't look the same, and I don't know how much we would be able to see from there in the first place. In the footage, you see that something was added and that there is some material in the room. I think it probably would not have been useful, and an analysis indicates something different. It would be useful in the final stage of analysis if it is shown that things could have been possible the way as described.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So a crime scene from almost 20 years before your visit is, as far as you know, on the basis of the information you have preserved and you determine that it wouldn't be useful to go to the crime scene to assess direction of fire? You did it on the basis of photographs instead; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no, no. I didn't say that. I only said that I suppose, in the meantime, the location changed. Now, as for the trace existing or not, we don't know that, and we don't know how we could ascertain that. If you look at the footage there is a room under construction, full of material. As for the nature of the damage and all the rest, that is a separate matter. Even in Barry Hogan's footage, he marked a location but it is not very clear that it is precisely the trace of a bullet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you didn't want to go there to see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wanted to see it, but then we realised that the place itself is not visible from Spicasta Stijena which was the basic precondition to any further discussion in deciding whether the bullet came from Spicasta Stijena or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ah-hah. So you didn't -- you went first to Spicasta Stijena to identify the incident site rather than to the area of the incident site?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And then we went to the location itself. We were at the location as well. But we were not looking for the trace that you referred to. I doubt we would have been able to identify it given the room and the amount of material. All sorts of damage is possible under such circumstances. How could have we been able to determine which one was the trace? In any case, in the footage it is quite low. That's the only relevant thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So just -- you've just mentioned that you determined that the incident site was not visible from Spicasta Stijena but that evidence certainly doesn't exclude the possibility that there was a line of site from Spicasta Stijena in 1993, at the time of the incident?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It excludes the possibility, because one cannot see Spicasta Stijena from the location because of nearby building which existed at the time. The girl itself in one of her statements said that she and her mother thought originally that they could not be hit from Spicasta Stijena. They believed that there was no line of sight. The building which hindered the view of Spicasta Stijena existed at the time. No one provided any evidence that the building did not exist at the time. We do not have such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 65 ter number 24147? It's a photo taken from the area of Sedrenik on 18 August 1993, from Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Date of the photo again, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 18 August -- pardon me, 18 August 1996, 18 August 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise, having taken photographs of the area of Sedrenik from Spicasta Stijena, do you recognise the general area? And by the way, the photo was taken at a magnification of 200.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you enlarge the upper part?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last part of the sentence. The witness trailed off.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, the interpreters didn't hear the last part of your sentence after you said, "Could you enlarge the upper part."

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the witness's house without the addition on it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I invite you to take a marker and indicate which house you're able to identify? I remember from your examination-in-chief you became quite skilled with the marker.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will mark it with a 1. Do you want me to mark the house?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think you could probably put a circle around the house as well as the 1.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you agree based on this photo from 1996, so much more contemporaneous to the date of the incident, that there is a much clearer line of sight at that time than there was when you took your photos in 2010?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only difference is concerning the terrace. What is important, though, is that the building existed - it still does - the one that is only partially visible from Spicasta Stijena. We mentioned what the distance of the building was supposed to be for the girl to be hit at such a low height as compared to Spicasta Stijena. What is important is that the building you can see in our photograph existed at the time as well. The one I'm marking it with 2. That building existed then and exists now. It covers the view of the location.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. But you haven't answered my question. My question was: Do you agree that a much clearer line of sight existed at that time than was the case when you took your photos in 2010?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see -- well, it's not necessarily a matter of line of sight. You say that the magnification here was 200 whereas we worked with 5. We don't see the entire door. We only see it partially. The girl was wounded in a squatting position, so very low, up to half a metre at the most. At that height, she could not have been hit from Spicasta Stijena. It is true, we can see it, as we can see it in the photograph, but we cannot see the ground floor. At least I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this as a Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we ask the witness to date and initial this photo?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, of course. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you be able to do that, Mr. Poparic?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Today is 4th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6362, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much more would you need to conclude your cross-examination, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would need the rest of the day. And probably after lunch I could provide Your Honours with a more accurate estimate of what I might be requesting in terms of time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But do you know how much time in total the Prosecution has spent so far for the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For the cross-examination related to the two reports, it is over five hours, Your Honours, and I do recall the order that Your Honours issued with respect to time before Mr. Poparic began his testimony. I would note, should Your Honours be inclined to reconsider, that Dr. Karadzic took far and away in excess of the five hours that he had originally estimated for his examination-in-chief, and although Dr. Karadzic spent almost no time, if I recall, on the inconsistencies report in the examination-in-chief, the cross-examination on that report occupied I think the better part of two hours. Virtually the entire examination-in-chief was about sniping incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton. Do your best to conclude your cross today. We will have a break --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- for 45 minutes and resume at 1.17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this is Pauline Wilson from Australia, one of our interns who will be joining us during this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, I'd like to move on to another incident now and it's incident F4, that's the first one that you spoke about in your examination-in-chief, and it's at paragraphs 53 to 61 of your report. And just a couple of brief questions: In paragraph 59, when you say that the line shifted towards Ivana Krndelja Street by about 100 metres, your basis for that is the pencil mark on the cut-out of the 1995 dated map we discussed earlier today; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. But when we come to the site itself, then we see that it couldn't have been any different in view of the configuration of the terrain. It either could have been there or up there in Ozrenska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for that, but I want you to focus on my questions. My next question about that map is: Do you know who made the pencil mark?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see. I cannot see the map. I can't see anything actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's in your report.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Image 49.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the map that was cited. The working map of the Chief of Staff of the 12th Division, Risoplek [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One question: You don't know who made the pencil mark, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see those markings in blue and red. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. I was referring to the pencil mark, but that's fine. Rather than spend any more time on this, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a straight line, if that's what you mean. I don't know. I did not mark anything on this map, if that's of any assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 65 ter number 25078, please, next. And page 1 of 25078. You can just make one photo of it and you can enlarge it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, this is one of the photos used with the victim in this case, during her testimony in this incident, during her testimony in the Galic case, and this has her hand drawn renderings of anti-sniper barricades and she has marked what she believes to be the origin of fire in this case with an X. That's at the top of the horizon, and then the location where she was shot and where she crawled with her daughter to rescue. You never actually went to that precise location on the horizon marked with an X to see whether the scene of the incident was actually visible; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there are photographs that we took there and the report -- in the report. And we checked whether there was visibility. Visibility is something that was dealt with in a considerable part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Let's look at D666 and this is a photo, a marked photo, from the scene of -- of the scene of the incident, which Mr. van der Weijden took from the area identified and marked by the witness with the X on the horizon of the photograph in front of us, D666 - if we could enlarge it, please - so Mr. van der Weijden went up to the location identified by the witness as the origin of fire and he took this photo from Ozrenska Street at street level standing on the sidewalk between the houses, and he marked the incident site in blue with number 1. So Mr. Poparic, if you had gone to that location, you would have seen that even today there is a clear line of sight to the spot where Mrs. Taric and her daughter were shot.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The photographs that are presented in the report, image 45, show -- or rather, the left-hand photograph shows the level at which the buildings can be seen at Hrasno Brdo and the photograph on the right-hand side that was taken from a bigger distance, actually, the building cannot be seen in Hrasno Brdo including Jagorska Street. I don't know where Mr. Weijden took this photograph from because this is zoomed in so I don't know exactly where it was taken from.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, the GPS co-ordinates where he took the photograph from are on the top. Right there, so --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These co-ordinates do not say a thing about the photograph. They speak about the place where he did the measuring but we don't have a photograph that shows -- I mean, a normal image so we can see where it was taken from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because we do not have the image with us -- on the English version does not have the image, can we see the image 45 the witness referred to?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's on page 75 of his report. 1D7902. Oh, you have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what did you say about this, Mr. Poparic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that these GPS co-ordinates do not say a thing about the photograph itself. They say something about the place where the photograph was taken. I don't know how Mr. Weijden could go to that place, according to the sketch, as it is marked there. It is a fact that there are photographs from another place from which the incident site is visible and I assume that Mr. van der Weijden took photographs from there. In the first photograph where the victim indicated the direction, we can just take this in tentative terms because she could not have known exactly where the fire had come from. She can just say where the fire came from in a general sense. Mr. Weijden's photograph is just zoomed in. I don't know where it was taken from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 25078, please, marked as a Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I don't mind it being marked for some limited purpose but I don't think it would be right to take this as the evidence of what the victim has asserted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit it to the extent necessary to understand the -- this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The only purpose for which it was offered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6363, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now I want to go on to an incident at a location we have talked about a couple of times, or we've talked about a couple of times today, and that's the sniping incident that took place on Brijesce Brdo, incident F5. And you've said a couple of times today that you went to that incident site, so you would agree with me, having gone there, that that incident location is at the end of a natural tunnel with the -- a line of sight blocked on the right-hand side by a hill with a radio tower and on the left-hand side by an elevation supported with a concrete wall. Having been there, I'm sure you would be able to agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly. If you meant the left side, we are talking about towards Rajlovac, towards the depot in Rajlovac, that side. On that side, there is this hill, this pile of earth, and it's not visible from the direction of Rajlovac, wouldn't be clear, or, rather, the western side, let us be --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Madam Interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let me help you, Mr. Poparic. If we could go to page 80 of your report, image 50.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the right side of this photograph, that can be seen, the transmission line, the pole, that's the western side. On that location, that's where the depot is, the railway depot in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, you would agree with me, looking at this image, that any potential field of fire is bounded by this tunnel, this natural tunnel; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Then I'd like to go over to image 53 in your report that is at page 85, where you map out what you see as the potential field of fire, using Google earth. But, Mr. Poparic, my concern is looking at the tunnel we've just seen that your markings actually double up the actual potential field of fire from the incident site, and you ignored, when you made those markings, the existence of the natural tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And before answering, if you could go to the enlarged box on the top right-hand corner of your photo, you see that marking, the boundary line furthest to the right, even crosses over the top of the natural tunnel that we saw on the left-hand side of the picture which was image 50.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, because in that area the slope is rather steep, and you can see across that, that's the reason why it's there. So let us correct that, too, by 2 degrees again. Basically it doesn't change anything. Even 5 degrees basically doesn't change anything. In order to see what the situation is on the ground -- of course, all of this should be taken as not being exactly accurate but there cannot be much deviation, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Then I'd like us to have a look at 65 ter 25129, which is, Mr. Poparic, your image 53 with Mr. van der Weijden's measured image of the potential field of fire from that incident location transposed over the top in green. The top image on this 65 ter number in light green shows the measured field of fire from Mr. van der Weijden's report, P1620 at page 35, overlaid on top of your markings. It represents, Mr. Poparic, not a minor deviation but it shows, as I put to you, that your assessed field of fire actually ignores the natural reality on the ground and doubles up what actually exists.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Absolutely not. Nothing is being denied in any way. As you see here, what I marked is basically -- well, actually even this area that I marked is perhaps wider than the one marked by Mr. Weijden except Mr. Weijden did not mark what was visible from BH Army positions. He dealt with one side only. If there is some deviation, it's not significant. The point is that we are not denying the fact that fire could have been opened from the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska because no one precisely specified the location involved. My report didn't, Mr. Weijden's report is not denying the fact that fire could have been opened from the direction of the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska except that Mr. van der Weijden did not deal with the possibility of fire having been opened from the positions of the BH Army. That is the essence of this matter. Now, whether I made a mistake by 2 degrees or whether he did, I think -- I mean, it doesn't really matter here because the exact location is unknown. The only important thing is whether it was possible to open fire from there, and yes that possibility did exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this as a Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, I'm not sure that it was recorded, line 14, that the witness said that he meant that from the Muslim side, I mean that fire could have been opened from the Muslim side too. The entire spectrum that he provided provided for that possibility too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, you may take up that issue in your re-examination. I think the transcript is clear enough at the moment. Yes, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6364, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go over to another area of Sarajevo and that's in Hrasno, and I'd like to ask you about scheduled sniping incident F10. And - I'm sorry - I'll just get you the paragraph numbers. Paragraph 134 of your report, going all the way over to paragraph 146. Now, in relation to this incident, you don't know -- you don't actually know where the Przulj house is, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reference to where the Przulj house is. It says that it's in Zagorska Street that is now called Posavska. On the spot we tried to find the house, and we identified a house that -- that is at the end of this street, that is dominant in that area, and we assumed that that was the house. The lady who owned the house could not confirm to us whether -- actually, what the name of the owner was, but she said that the house had been seriously damaged and that they even changed that side of the house that was facing the centre of Sarajevo, rather Cengic Vila, so we assumed that that is the only house that could have been dominant and from where fire could have been opened in view of what was seen on the spot. No one identified it as being the exact house concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, you said, in your testimony in chief, that based on your image which is image 89 at page 128 of your report, the damage to the awning of the area cafe wasn't a bullet trace, and in your report you're actually more specific. You argued that the bullet-hole that we see in image 89 was probably made by a screwdriver, and the dark spot on the wide angle photo of the cafe, which is image 88, is the real bullet-hole. So just to be clear, the only basis you have for saying that the enlarged left-hand photo on image 89 is a bullet-hole is that photo; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is claimed on the basis of photo documentation and we showed this in this photograph, and the second basis is my vast experience precisely with hits in several targets. I saw hundreds or thousands of such hits and the penetration that is shown here with an arrow that the police identified as a bullet-hole is not a bullet-hole. I claim that with full responsibility. This is some kind of mechanical damage sustained by the awning, and in my view the police misidentified the place where the bullet entered the awning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's based on your examination of this photo; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The examination of the photo and the familiarity with the characteristics of the bullet which pierces fabric or cloth of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. So can you explain why, for example, looking at the real bullet-hole, the left hand picture, of image 89, explain why you can be sure that that left-hand image isn't a crease or a piece of dirt or a shadow or a puckered stitch or bird dropping or some other dark spot on the basis of that photo?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I took all that into consideration. However, if it is true, and it is true, that the glass was shattered, that the bullet pierced the glass, it had to exit the awning at some place and the only place we saw is this place and it corresponds to the characteristics of a bullet piercing an awning of this kind. This was not done subsequently. This is a hole probably produced by a bullet. And in terms its size, the size of the opening, it may be assessed that this was indeed a bullet or a projectile.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's based on your analysis of these photos that you came up with an angle of descent for the bullet of 45 degrees; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to say something with a reservation. We could not be precise because we did not have all the measurements. This is an estimate. The descent angle was rather large and that drastically differs from a descent angle of a bullet if such a bullet had been fired from positions in Zagorska-Posavska Street, as it is known now. If it had been fired from Zagorska, the descent angle would have been 4 to 5 degrees and here it is much larger. It doesn't really matter whether it is 45, 35 or 50. It doesn't really matter. What matters is that it deviates drastically from an angle it would have had if the bullet had been fired from a position in Zagorska Street, and that is how things should be interpreted in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. So if we assume in this case that the witnesses who told the investigators that the shots came in immediately one after the other are accurate, the conclusion we would draw from your analysis is that the victim was fired on from one position and at almost the exact same time a stray bullet that someone else fired in the air landed in almost the exact same place going through the awning and the window; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would not say that. I wouldn't deal with that. I'm not sure that there were two bullets which were fired at the same time. We have to bear in mind the sequence of events. The police came, the boy was transferred to the hospital. Based on the traces on the awning, they stated that the bullet had come from Zagorska Street. I cannot be sure that that was created on that particular day. Maybe it preexisted the event. We don't have any information about that. All the options are possible. Maybe the bullets were fired from the same weapon on the same day, maybe these two events are not connected at all. In any case, the police erred in the identification of the entry hole in the awning, and there is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's assume actually that it happened on the same day at the same time as the witnesses say. That would mean that your stray bullet would have had to have made a turn in mid-air after it went through the awning because otherwise coming out of the sky at a 45-degree angle it would be impossible for it to have gone through the cafe and hit the cafe wall at the back; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That's not correct. It could have travelled that route without any problems. Based on the traces we established that the angle was 45 degrees. There is no doubt about that. If this is the entry point as given in image on the left-hand side, then the descent angle of the bullet that hit the cafe is what it was. There is a photo depicting the boy's wounds. Actually, not the wounds themselves, but in any case, it's very hard to say based on that photo that the boy was hit by a bullet that followed that trajectory and descended that the angle.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Talking about the boy, actually, you stated in your report that the boy wasn't shot in front of the cafe, and so what I'd like to know -- and by the way that was at paragraph 144 of your report. So what I'd like to know is what is your theory about how the big pool of blood that was on the ground in front of the cafe came to be there?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, nobody said that he was shot in front of the cafe. Second of all, he was shot across the street near a shop. What you say that there was a pool of blood there, it seems to me that there was some water, at least judging by the photo that I had. The boy sustained a very small wound. I really don't see how that wound could have created such a big pool of what you say is blood. He had a slight wound and he was transferred to the hospital immediately. The pool of blood is too big to have been caused by such a small wound.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's your personal opinion, isn't it, because you're not a doctor?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a doctor. However, based on the photo, that looked -- looks like water to me. The photos are not very good. However, I paid a lot of attention to that data, and I believe that it was a pool of water, not a pool of blood.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. We'll go on to another incident because you talked about all of them in your evidence-in-chief, and this incident is F16, and you deal with it in your report at paragraphs 191 through to 197. Now, as I understand your claim about this incident in your report, you say that based on the picture you have in figure 110, image 110, you assume that Mr. Agovic was seated facing directly forward in his seat at a 45-degree angle vis-a-vis the tram, and as a result, for the bullet to have entered his left side and exited his right side, it had to have been fired from an angle of 45 degrees or less. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. What is a characteristic is the chair where the wounded person was sitting. In this case, it is placed at 45 -- at a 45-degree angle. It is to be assumed that his sitting position was normal. There is no data showing that he was sitting in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So you have no idea how he was actually seated at the time, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only know that he was seated. It is to be assumed that his sitting position was normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. We can actually leave that incident and move on. Criss-crossing the city of Sarajevo, I'd like to deal with an incident in Nedzarici, and that's sniping incident F7. And you address that at paragraphs 93 all the way through to 111 of your report. Now, with regard to this incident, you said in your evidence-in-chief that you went to the faculty of theology in Nedzarici and while you were there you got some photos and it was clear from those photos that there were some firing positions but it was impossible to see the incident site from there. You said that at transcript pages 38969 and 38972. And that was because, as I understand your report, a tree was blocking the line of sight; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The tree was there and it was blocking the line of sight partially. However, what we can see here are only the houses, or rather, their roofs. Owing to the tree, we managed to come up with the analysis of the position of the school of theology and the place where the bus was and we show it in image 69. We can see that this is the place where the school of theology was, and that it is lower than the place where the bus was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's stick with the tree for a moment. Could we have a look at page 103 of your report?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Image 67. Could we enlarge image 67? All right. So first of all, the gun holes that we see in this photo facing us in the wall of the faculty of theology, don't -- have no exposure to the incident site; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I said that that side was facing Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually in the text box under your photograph you say it's facing Vojnicko Polje.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one and the same. Vojnicko Polje and Alipasino Polje are next to each other, following each other on the same axis, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Are you able to mark on this photograph where you took the photo which is image 67A from? Where on this building, the faculty of theology, did you take that photo with the tree from?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I marked that with number 1. I was on the terrace and I turned in the direction of the place of the incident. This is the direction from which the photo was taken, or rather the direction towards which the photo was taken here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So just if I can just a moment, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For the record the witness has circled and marked with a number 1 a terrace or balcony on image 67 as being the location that he took image 67A from, and with an arrow marking number 2 he's indicated where he had to turn to take that photo from.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I interrupted you but I think you hadn't finished your sentence.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to explain why we took the photo from that terrace, because we had assumed that the firing position may have been on a window on that side, which means that the view that we had corresponded to a possible firing position on a window facing Dobrinja and the place of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're not trying to say that because a tree blocked your line of sight in 2010, that we should infer that there was no line of sight 16 years earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained that. In order to eliminate those suspicions we carried out an additional analysis based on the elevations where those places, those two places, are. We confirmed that the level from which the photo was taken almost matched the level of the place where the bus was. Since there are a lot of buildings --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't want you to repeat yourself. So this analysis that you made, as to the potential firing position, completely excludes the possibility that the shot in this case could have come from the roof, for example; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It could not have come from a roof. When we were taking the photo I would like to say that I did not take photos at the level of the openings but from my height, I'm about 172, and the roof is 1 to 1 and a half metre higher than that; however, that would not have impacted the visibility at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So can you explain in --before we go further, could I have this image marked as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours? Could you sign it and date it, please, Mr. Poparic?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6365, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you talked in your report and in your evidence-in-chief about the difference in altitude or elevation between the specific incident site and location on the faculty of theology, what does that practically mean? Does that mean that you couldn't see the incident site from anywhere on the faculty of theology?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. We could not see it from anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Because of the difference in altitude or elevation?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been a subsequent explanation of the fact. We simply did not see it on the day because it could not be seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you're not excluding the possibility that there was a line of sight from the faculty of theology to the incident location on the date of the incident, 25 May 1994, are you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completely exclude that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a look at another photograph. It's 65 ter 25124. This is a photo, Mr. Poparic, taken on 17 August 1996, and you could see the date on the bottom right-hand corner of the film, from the top floor of the faculty of theology, and if my colleague can enlarge the space between the apartment buildings on the right-hand side of the picture. And again, Mr. Poparic, you see in front of you a clear line of sight down the street towards the incident location where the bus was hit on the 25 May 1994. So it looks like you were wrong.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photo has been zoomed in. We don't know where it was taken from. According to what I saw, in and around the school of theology, this photo could not have been taken from there. Look at photo 67. You will see that a similar image is not seen from there. Even if there was line of visibility, you could only see above what we see now, above the line of what we see now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You're disputing -- you're disputing that this photo was taken from the faculty of theology? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not convinced that it was taken from the faculty of theology.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And are you disputing that the path through these two apartment buildings or these apartment buildings, the street that we see, is the street down which the bullet flew on 25 May 1994 to hit the bus?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can this part here be zoomed in where we can see the street next to the white building? Can you zoom in, please? Okay. What doesn't make sense to me here is the fact that in the background you can't see any other buildings. There is no single building there, although we know that there indeed is a building in the background. I can't recognise this area. There are a lot of similar buildings in Dobrinja so I wouldn't be sure that that is the street in question. There should be another building across the street in which the bus was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just to underscore, you were never in Dobrinja during the war, you have no idea, then, what the terrain and features would have been like in 1996?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a very good idea. I'm familiar with Dobrinja as it was before the war. All of those buildings were built before the war. This white building at the end of it is a street and across the street there is another building which was built before the war. That was the first part of Dobrinja that was ever built, and that happened before the war, and I can't see that building here. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. We'll deal with this with another witness. I'd like to go now still -- your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour. I'd like to go over to scheduled incident F12, which you dealt with in paragraphs 162 to 174 of your report. That's the incident dealing with the sniping death of Nermin Divovic and his mother -- the injury of his mother, Mrs. Dzenana Sokolovic. Now, with respect to this incident, you make the inference that Nermin Divovic and his mother were caught in a cross-fire. You do that in paragraphs 173 and 174 of your report. If you could just clarify something for me, you base that inference solely on the film that we saw in your evidence-in-chief; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, there is no evidence of any gunfire other than what we hear on that film, Mr. Poparic, so can you identify this specific source apart from that film that you relied on to support your inference that they were caught in the cross-fire?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a statement by Dzenana Sokolovic. She provided it in 2006, I believe. In that statement, she clearly stated that when she had left Hrasno Brdo and when she had arrived close to the municipal building, the building of the municipality of Nova Sarajevo, she heard shots, everybody lied down, and she felt that she had been hit, that her son fell on the ground. This is what Mrs. Sokolovic said. I don't know whether it's accurate or not. I can't be the judge of that. However, we have to take into consideration that option as well. That's why we said that there was a possibility that that was how things happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, first of all, just to deal with what you've said, you've just told the Chamber that Dzenana Sokolovic in a statement said that when they arrived close to the municipal building, the building of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, she heard shots. She never in her statement referred to the building of the Novo Sarajevo municipality. It's your analysis that that's the building she referred to; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it wasn't translated well. I simply provided an additional comment. She said the municipal building and it was my comment that it was the municipal building of Novo Sarajevo municipality. That is the only municipal building on her route. That was my comment to her statement, just to make that clear. Perhaps there was a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. So leaving her statement aside, which -- no, actually let's deal with her statement. In this statement, it's correct, isn't it, that despite whatever municipal building she might have referred to, Dzenana Sokolovic identified the Metalka building as the origin of fire.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. Ultimately she did but --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But what? Yes, please continue, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To continue? She identified it. However, what is not disputed, that she on different occasions provided different statements. In my view, it cannot be easily overlooked. She also only identified it. She did not provide a clear indication which would convince us that her assessment was correct. It may well be her assessment but it is undisputed that she provided different statements. That is why we need to take all that into account, and it makes that case that much more complicated, because of the contradictory documentation pertaining to medical records, the witness statements, et cetera. That's the problem of that particular case. We cannot identify the reliable information. That's the underlying problem. Forensic medication -- forensic analysis, forensic documentation would have resolved many an issue but it was unavailable to me. There is only that excerpt from the autopsy report. I don't know exactly what was done, but it was far from sufficient. It only contradicts what --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All you're doing is repeating the contents of your report now and to get back on track to my original question regarding cross-fire, I'd like ask you this: You don't exclude that any reports of gunfire following the injury of Mrs. Sokolovic could have come from UNPROFOR's anti-sniping teams responding to the source of fire, do you? You don't exclude that at all?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing can be excluded. That's the problem in the case. The case is problematic because we have data which is not always reliable and that could be used to exclude something that is not reliable, obviously some of it is unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at another document, 65 ter 11359. And unfortunately I don't think it's available in B/C/S. This is an UNPROFOR daily sit-rep for 18 November 1994 -- oh, it is. How nice. In English -- we will just wait a moment. If we could go over to English page 8, I'll try and find the corresponding paragraph number so we can go to the appropriate page in the B/C/S. English page 8, paragraph 3. So if we could find paragraph 3 in the B/C/S version, this is a report on events in, among many other places, Sarajevo for the 18th of November, 1994. And in subparagraph (a) that you see in the top of the page in English, it says: "In the area of the Tito barracks, a sniping incident left a 5-year-old child dead and his mother injured. The origin of the fire was Bosnian Serb army, FreeBat 4 --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, do we have it in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think what you need to do is go -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't realise there was a translation or else I would have indicated the paragraph numbers. I think we need to go further in the page. Could we go over to the next page in B/C/S, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's page 11 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, and apologies. Top paragraph on the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the last sentence reads: "The original of the fire was BSA, FreeBat 4 returned 14.5 millimetre fire." Do you find that a reliable report, Mr. Poparic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the witness. Could he please be asked to speak clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, could you repeat your answer more clearly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no reason to question its reliability. However, in the report it is stated that fire was opened close to the Marsal Tito barracks. That could also be a location or the location. I have no reason to distrust it. It addresses somewhat more the origin of fire in this incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So then you don't exclude the possibility that rather than an exchange of fire, what might have been going on was the UNPROFOR anti-sniping teams neutralising the origin of fire in Bosnian Serb-held territory?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It tells me that fire was open on both sides. As for the real reason of it, that is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It seems that the B/C/S version does not correspond to the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then my mistake. No. I think we have correct page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think so. If I can read it in my poor accent in B/C/S, it reads: [Interpretation] "In the area of Tito Barracks a sniping incident left a 5-year-old child dead and his mother insured. The origin of the fire was BSA. FreeBat 4 returned 14.5 millimetre fire." [In English] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, on its face this document does not say anything about fire being opened on both sides. It talks about UNPROFOR neutralising the source of fire on Bosnian Serb-held territory. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that that is what we find in the document. It is also true that in the footage that was shown, one could hear bursts of fire. However, judging by the footage I wouldn't say it was 14.5-millimetre calibre, it was a smaller weapon. This case cannot be resolved based on documents such as this one. It can be used as an aid but the main point would be forensic analysis. It would be of great assistance if we knew the height of the wound in the case of the lady wounded on the left side, and the one wounded on the right side. That would have been of assistance but we don't have that. Documents such as this one can give us a general picture but they do not resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If this in the witness's view could be used for an aid, I'd like to have it as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6366, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to deal with the tram sniping incident next, Mr. Poparic. And that's incident F11, from October 1994. And you can find it at paragraphs 147 right through to 161 of your report. Now, you've written extensively about this in your report and I want to focus on a couple of points from your argument. As I understand your contention, you say that there was a shooter in the Executive Council building who was firing on these trams, and because there were two hit that day and who fired on passers-by on the street afterwards. Do I understand it correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. It is obvious from the traces left behind by the bullets hitting the ground, there was a plume of dust created at a sharp angle. It could only have been created by an angle of descent of a projectile and the bullet had a high force causing dust to rise into the air, and that in turn means it was fired from a short distance away.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. Now, your evidence on these dust clouds that you gave in your report, and by the way that's at paragraph 161 of the report, your evidence about these dust clouds, that's not based on any published studies or trials or anything like that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
